transcript:
This message comes from University at Buffalo, where scientists are working to protect the Great Lakes and fresh water supplies around the world from harmful contamination.
Learn more about their research at buffalo.edu/npr.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. There are multiple victims after a shooting today at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon.
Bend Police Department spokesperson Sheila Miller says the suspect is dead.
We received the first report at 1259 of a shooter outside of the building shooting into a car.
And within about a minute, we were receiving multiple 911 calls from within the school.
Miller said the attacker was shot and went down inside the school soon after police arrived. It was not immediately clear if it was by police, a bystander or self-inflicted.
The death toll is preliminary and could change.
The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are looking into a series of suspicious mailings sent to congressional offices in some states.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wong reports some of the mailings contained a powdery white substance.
It's not clear who sent the mail to election officials in states including Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma.
Deputy Chief Inspector Brendan Donahue says the U.S. Postal Inspection Service was able to stop the delivery of at least one of the mailings.
Some of the letters have contained an unknown substance and we're working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident.
With less than three weeks until November 3rd, voting officials around the country are working to carry out the midterm elections.
The investigation has not stopped early voting. In a statement, the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors say,
"Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties."
Hansi Lo Wong, NPR News.
FBI employees fired for their roles in the investigation of President Trump's retention of classified documents at his Florida estate are suing to get their jobs back.
The complaint adds to the legal challenges to mass firings under FBI Director Cash Patel. Agents say they were wrongly fired for participating in investigations of Trump or are seen as opposed to Trump administration interests.
Patel says employees he has fired had weaponized the FBI.
A study finds that ultra-processed foods overall do not increase a person's risk of developing colorectal cancer.
But as NPR's Maria Godoy reports, the risk varied depending on the type of food.
The majority of industrially made packaged foods sold in grocery stores count as ultra-processed, from jarred pasta sauces to sugary drinks.
In this study, researchers looked at data from more than 460,000 U.S. adults between the ages of 50 and 71 over nearly two decades.
They found that eating processed meats was linked to a higher risk of colorectal cancer.
But a higher intake of other foods from the ultra-process category, specifically whole grains and dairy, was associated with a lower risk.
The researchers say the findings support current recommendations to consume whole grains, fiber, dairy and calcium and avoid processed meats.
The findings appear in the journal PLOS Medicine. Maria Godoy and PR News.
Since major U.S. stock indexes closed higher today, the S&P 500 rose more than a quarter percent, the Dow rose more than one percent.
This is NPR.
Lawyers for the BBC say that President Trump is trying to delay sitting for a deposition in the defamation case he brought against the British broadcaster.
Trump has a history of avoiding depositions.
He filed the lawsuit against the BBC last December, seeking $10 billion in damages.
In a filing this week, the BBC asked a Florida court to compel Trump to appear.
High housing costs are on the ballot in Massachusetts.
NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports voters will decide whether the state should join others in creating starter homes on smaller lots.
In Massachusetts, most single-family homes must sit on at least an acre of land, nearly the size of a football field without the end zones.
Economist Andrew Mikula says it's fueled a housing shortage and an exodus of working-age people.
That not only separates extended families, but also hurts our economy.
A ballot measure would allow homes built on smaller lots about the size of a basketball court.
But Jill Hay, a select board member in the wealthy town of Lexington, doubts it will help first-time buyers there.
The lot size is not what's going to drive affordability.
In this market, she says even smaller new homes are going for $1 million and more.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Lexington, Massachusetts.
Manhattan's Upper West Side has new celebrity residents, a family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park.
An expert says this is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history.
The owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street, eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds.
I'm Rylan Barton. This is NPR News from Washington.
This message comes from IXL, a learning platform for helping kids build confidence and get up to speed fast.

FBI and Postal Inspection Service probe suspicious mailings with powder sent to congressional and election offices
FBI employees fired over Trump classified documents investigation sue to regain their jobs
Study finds ultra-processed foods overall not linked to colorectal cancer risk, but processed meats are

President Trump tries to delay deposition in $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC
